canonical_topic: Regulated power markets and integrated utilities
definition: In regulated (non-deregulated) power grids, a monopoly utility that owns both transmission and generation (an integrated utility) is typically the sole supplier of power to consumers within its service area, overseen by a government commission that sets consumer prices.
core_idea: Because the integrated utility is the sole supplier, there is little or no wholesale market inside the service area; any trading happens only at the import/export interconnection points with neighboring systems.
key_points: The overseeing body is usually called a public utility commission or public service commission.
Trading nodes at the edges of a regulated utility's territory typically have names describing the interconnection, e.g., 'Into-Southern Company' or 'Into-Dominion'.
The commission determines the consumer electricity prices the utility may charge.
relationships: Contrasts with deregulated SMD markets that use node/zone/hub LMP pricing and active wholesale trading.
trading_implications: Wholesale trading opportunities in a regulated market are effectively limited to the utility's import/export interface points, not internal delivery points.
caveats: Not all power grids are deregulated — deregulated wholesale market mechanics (nodal LMPs, hub trading) don't apply inside a regulated integrated utility's service territory.
